text:
Hidasi and Karatzoglou’s CIKM 2018 paper provides direct GRU4Rec precedent for changing both loss and negative sampling. Ordinary BPR/TOP1 dilute useful gradients when many negatives are easy; BPR-max and TOP1-max emphasize high-scoring negatives through softmax weights. With positive score r+, negative scores rj, and sj=softmax(rj), regularized BPR-max is −log Σj sj·sigmoid(r+−rj) + λΣj sj·rj². TOP1-max instead softmax-weights the TOP1 pairwise losses, but retains their sensitivity to large scores. The paper reports improvements up to 35% over previous session-based RNN solutions; these are not Amazon benchmark results. [Paper](https://hidasi.eu/assets/pdf/gru4rec_v2_cikm18.pdf)

The official implementation supports in-batch negatives plus additional samples drawn with probability proportional to item frequency^α: α=0 gives uniform sampling, α=1 popularity sampling. Its guidance suggests 2,048 additional negatives, reduced for catalogs below roughly 5–10K items. Both cross-entropy and BPR-max remain recommended objectives; cross-entropy generally benefits from logQ correction (`logq=1`), added in 2020 rather than the 2018 paper. Published repository configurations favor different losses on different datasets. Inference for this search: sampled cross-entropy is a defensible first experiment, but evidence does not establish it as best for the four Amazon categories. Compare it against regularized BPR-max using a controlled sampling setup and the fixed macro validation HR@10; retain one GRU model per category throughout. [Official implementation and guidance](https://github.com/hidasib/GRU4Rec)
